Victim
VIK-tim
noun
From Latin victima — a beast appointed for sacrifice, the animal brought to the altar. The word entered English through sacrificial religion and only later widened to mean any person destroyed or injured by another's act. The oldest meaning still governs the deepest one: at the center of the faith stands a true Victim, the Lamb appointed before the foundation of the world.

📖 Biblical Definition

One who actually suffers wrong at the hands of another — the man stripped and left half dead on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30), Abel whose blood cried from the ground (Gen. 4:10), Naboth under false witnesses, Uriah under a king's pen. Scripture never blinks at the reality of victims: God names himself "the helper of the fatherless" (Psa. 10:14), hears the cry of the afflicted widow (Ex. 22:22-23), and prices the blood of the poor as "precious... in his sight" (Psa. 72:14). Biblical justice exists in large part FOR victims — open thy mouth for the dumb (Prov. 31:8) — and the avenger-of-blood and cities of refuge were a whole legal architecture built around innocent blood. But Scripture does two further things the age refuses to do together: it insists victimhood is a wrong suffered, not a righteousness possessed — the victim needs Christ's blood exactly as his oppressor does — and it refuses to let victimhood be destiny: Joseph, the Bible's archetypal victim, ends the story saying "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Gen. 50:20). The supreme Victim is Christ himself — oppressed, afflicted, opening not his mouth (Isa. 53:7), reviled yet not reviling (1 Pet. 2:23) — who did not weaponize his wounds but redeemed through them, and rose.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828: a living being sacrificed to some deity or in a religious rite; something destroyed or sacrificed in the pursuit of an object; a person destroyed or grievously injured by another.

expand to see more

VICTIM, noun. A living being sacrificed to some deity, or in the performance of a religious rite; usually, some beast slain in sacrifice; but human beings have been slain by some nations, for the purpose of appeasing the wrath or conciliating the favor of some deity.

Something destroyed; something sacrificed in the pursuit of an object.

A person or thing destroyed or sacrificed by, or suffering grievous injury from, another; as a victim of fraud, of oppression, of war.

Note the order: Webster's first sense is sacrificial. The word's center of gravity is the altar, not the grievance.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 4:10 — "And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground."

Exodus 22:22-23 — "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry;"

Psalm 10:14 — "Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless."

Proverbs 31:8-9 — "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy."

Isaiah 53:7 — "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth."

Genesis 50:20 — "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."

1 Peter 2:23 — "Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The age corrupts the word from both ends — inflating victimhood into an identity and a currency, or cynically denying that real victims exist at all. Scripture rebukes both.

expand to see more

The first corruption is inflation. Where the word once named a wrong suffered, it now names a status held — renewable, rankable, and spendable. Grievance becomes capital; the standpoint theorists supply the epistemology (the victim sees truest — see [[standpoint-epistemology]]), the bureaucracies supply the incentives, and soon the title is claimed most loudly by those wronged least, while the actually crushed — the trafficked, the aborted, the persecuted church — are crowded out of their own category. When victimhood pays, counterfeits multiply; and every counterfeit cheapens the coin the real victim must spend to be heard.

The second corruption is the backlash that overcorrects: the sneer that 'there are no victims, only volunteers,' the reflex that every sufferer must have earned it. That is the theology of Job's friends, and God's verdict on it was wrath (Job 42:7). Scripture will not allow it: blood cries from the ground and God hears (Gen. 4:10); the widow's cry triggers his own avenging (Ex. 22:23-24). A man hardened against real victims is not based; he is unlike his God, who took up the victim's cause so personally that he became one.

The biblical balance is severe in both directions. To the wronged: your suffering is seen, priced, and will be requited — and it is a wound, not a crown; only one Victim's blood justifies, and it is not yours. To the comfortable: the test of pure religion remains the fatherless and the widow (James 1:27), and the mouth God commands you to open is for the dumb, not for yourself. The gospel's final word to victims is Joseph's and Christ's: wrong is real, God means it for good, and resurrection — not retribution and not curated grievance — is the end of the story.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin victima, the sacrificial beast — the word begins at the altar, climaxes at the Cross, and only degenerates into a status symbol when severed from both.

expand to see more

Latin: victima — the beast appointed for sacrifice; cognate with the religious vocabulary of consecration, not of complaint.

Hebrew (concept): anaw / ani (H6041) — the afflicted, poor, oppressed whom God defends; dam naqi, innocent blood, which the LORD will not hold guiltless.

Greek (concept): amnos (G286), the Lamb — "behold the Lamb of God" (John 1:29); the New Testament's victim-word is a sacrifice-word, fulfilled at the Cross.

KJV note: the English word 'victim' never appears in the KJV — Scripture speaks instead of the afflicted, the oppressed, the fatherless, and the Lamb, keeping persons and sacrifice distinct until they meet in Christ.

Usage

"The church must be the safest place on earth for a real victim and the hardest place on earth to profit from a fake claim — Prov. 31:8 and Prov. 18:17 in the same building."

"He suffered a genuine wrong, and the men around him made sure of two things: that justice was pursued, and that the wound never became his name."

"Christ is the only Victim whose wounds justify anyone — which frees the wronged man to seek justice without needing his suffering to be his righteousness."
